_README: Internal database jargon removed from rendered route prose: "on file" / "the on-file X", the enrichment pipeline referring to its own stored values in text a climber reads. Every number, place name, hazard and caveat is kept; only the framing changes. Findings that existed ONLY in a deleted note were checked against the live columns first and recorded in research-data/DEFECT-TRIAGE-2026-08-19-CLUSTERED.md.

set.rappel_count_note: The five stations are the DOUBLE-ROPE count. The same descent is not five rappels for everyone: a party taking many shorter rappels on a single rope logged 9-10 to reverse the route back to Burgundy Col, and a party on two 60 m ropes describes doubling up for the first, one single rappel to the ledge at the bottom of pitch 3, then three more double rappels to the col. Neither is wrong. Action Potential has no rappel line of its own - parties finish into North Face terrain near Burgundy Ledge and take that route's descent. On rope choice the published accounts disagree in a way worth knowing: two ropes are faster, but one first-hand account calls double ropes on this descent annoying and prone to getting stuck, and recommends a single 70 m instead - a single 60 m leaves you about 10 ft above the only bolted anchor on the route. Per-station distances are not published in any account read for this route; the figures given come from the route's own descent text rather than from measurement.

set.approach: From the Rachel Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft, end of FS Rd 4930 off Kachess Lake Rd, Exit 62 from I-90), start on Rachel Lake Trail #1313. The first ~2.75 miles follow Box Canyon Creek on gentle grade, crossing several side streams and cascades (reliable water throughout — no need to carry much from the car). At about mile 2.75 the trail crosses Box/Canyon Creek and hits the notorious 'mile from hell': a heavily rooted, rocky boot-beaten climb that gains roughly 1,300 ft in about a mile, with large step-ups and no switchbacks — this is the crux of the approach fitness-wise, not technically hard but brutal with a full pack. The trail tops out at Rachel Lake (4,700 ft, ~3.5-4 mi from the TH); a use trail/climber's path branches right near the outhouse and skirts the north side of the lake, then switchbacks steeply up rocky tread for about half a mile to the Rampart Ridge crest (~5,100 ft). At the ridge junction, go left (south) for Rampart Lakes or right for Lila Lake/Alta Mountain — for this route, follow the trail south along the ridge/east side of the Rampart Lakes basin. Stay on maintained tread through the lakes basin (it's fragile alpine turf/talus; short-cut social trails are discouraged and often marked closed with sticks/rock piles). At the south end of the lakes, locate the base of a large boulder gully with cliff bands on its left (west) side; ascend this gully on a boot path to a broad saddle at about 5,570 ft on the Rampart Ridge crest. Total to this point is roughly 6-6.5 miles and ~3,000 ft gain. From the saddle, turn west and follow the increasingly exposed climber's path along the ridge crest toward Alta's summit block, negotiating three false summits, class 2-3 rock steps, and short sections of real exposure (in one section the path skirts a cliff edge — fall consequences are serious here, and the route should not be attempted with snow on the ridge). A helmet is commonly recommended for the final ridge scramble due to loose rock and exposure. Total one-way distance to the 6,274 ft summit is about 9.5-10 km (matches the 19.3 km round trip) with roughly 3,300 ft of total gain.

Drive the Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead (roughly MP 20, ~2,100 ft) — note the flood-related closure near the park boundary that has, in recent years, added a bike or walk-in stretch to reach the actual trailhead. From the parking area, find the log crossing of the Cascade River near the Eldorado Creek confluence; the crossing has been rebuilt repeatedly after flood damage and can be an awkward single-log or jammed-log crossing depending on the year, so scout it before committing. On the far side, pick up the unsigned but well-trodden climbers' path, which pushes through swampy brush and devil's club before settling into open old-growth timber. The path gains roughly 1,500 ft through timber before breaking out onto the first of two wide boulder/talus fields (watch for marmots, and follow cairns/boot track for the path of least resistance through the rock). Above the talus the trail crosses an alpine meadow strewn with rocks and streams — climbers compare it to a smaller Boston Basin — then drops briefly before a slabby rock ramp leads up onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier. Rope up and crampon here. Parties camp either lower, at Eldorado Creek Basin (~5,600 ft) or Roush Creek Basin (~6,100–6,400 ft), or push on to a high camp near Eldorado's East Ridge/upper Eldorado Glacier (~7,200–7,600 ft) to shorten summit day; trailhead to high camp runs roughly 5–7 miles with about 5,500–6,000 ft of gain, typically 5–6+ hours. From high camp the route to Austera continues as sustained glacier travel rather than a trail: cross the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier (crevasses are worst near Eldorado's east ridge — stay roped and probe), traverse the upper Inspiration Glacier at ~7,800 ft to Klawatti Col, pass Klawatti Peak on its left through the col, and follow Klawatti's north ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 miles to a break in the ridge at ~7,900 ft — the Klawatti–Austera col/notch. This glacier traverse from camp to the base of Austera's southwest side is itself roughly 3 miles with real elevation swings (guide sources cite about 1,280 ft of ascent and 592 ft of descent over 2.8 miles, ~4 hours one-way), crossing three glacier basins and two cols, one of which (the Klawatti–Austera notch) is a technical crux: a moat gap at the col that often requires careful stemming or a short rappel to get down onto the upper Klawatti Glacier before the final traverse to Austera's base. Primary hazards throughout: crevasse fall on all three glaciers (worse as the season progresses and snow bridges soften), a genuinely committing and remote setting with long retreat times, loose rock ('choss') on any exposed rock sections, and route-finding difficulty in flat light or whiteout on the open ice cap.

From the FS 3160 road-end parking (roughly 48.957°N, 121.851°W, reached via Canyon Creek Road/FS 31 then FS 3160 as noted above), the route follows an unmaintained but well-worn boot path — not a numbered Forest Service trail, just a heavily used user track — that climbs steeply through forest for about 0.6-0.7 mile and roughly 400 ft of gain to Church Lake, a small emerald subalpine lake sitting in a cirque directly below Bearpaw's north side. This first pitch is the steepest sustained grade of the day. Skirt the lake along its east/left shore (best flat campsites are on the far side, useful if splitting the trip). Beyond the lake the trail fades into intermittent boot-path and cairns through meadows and heather benches; keep left (west) up the basin rim toward a broad saddle/high point around 6,066 ft on the ridge separating Church Lake's basin from Bearpaw's summit block — this stretch accounts for most of the remaining ~900 ft of the route's 1,300 ft total gain over roughly 1.5 mi one-way (matching the ~5.9 km round trip). From the 6,066 ft saddle, drop slightly and traverse north across a rocky/heather bowl toward the base of Bearpaw's summit block; the final approximately 300 ft to the 6,091 ft summit is easy class 2-3 scrambling on generally solid rock and blocks, with mild exposure in the last pitch. Church Lake is the last reliable water source — carry water from there for the upper mountain. There is no maintained tread past the lake, so route-finding by cairns and boot-path is necessary, and in early/mid-season lingering snow on the steep initial slope above the lake and in the summit gullies can require an ice axe and caution; several trip reports note snow patches into July on shaded sections.

From the FR 4096 spur (reached via Mountain Loop Highway to just past Bedal Campground, then up FR 4096), the actual hike starts at an unsigned, unmaintained climber's boot path around 2,100–2,200 ft, roughly 1.3 miles up the spur road near its second or third switchback. The trailhead is marked only by a small cairn/rock pile in the roadside grass and is notoriously easy to drive past — worth GPS-marking on the way in. The path drops into forest and follows Merry Brook (also called Merry Creek) upstream — the last reliable water on route — before swinging north out of the drainage to gain a forested ridge around 2,600 ft. Expect a genuinely unmaintained track with blowdown, brush, and a few faint braids; pink flagging tied roughly every 100 yards helps confirm you're on line, but parties still regularly lose the path, so download a GPS track before you go. Above the ridge the trail climbs through a first boulder field around 3,500 ft (moss-covered talus, easiest when snow-free), passes above a small tarn (Nels Lake) with a cascade audible below, then reaches a second boulder field near 4,200 ft that often holds snow into summer, with views opening north to Spring Mountain around 4,300 ft. By roughly 4,450 ft the route is typically on solid snow in early/mid-season. The technical crux comes around 4,900–5,200 ft at a cliff band below the summit massif: parties look for a ramp/notch line rather than the more direct gully (a moat-like gap has been found there and is best avoided), and the rock is mossy and loose in spots, occasionally icy where snow meets rock — a short hand-line is sometimes used here by less experienced climbers. A short descending traverse east through overgrown brush and devil's club near 5,200 ft regains the ridge above treeline, after which it's a straightforward snow climb and crossing of low-angle granite slabs to the east ridge — an easy, minimally-exposed Class 2–3 scramble toward the summit.

set.rappel_count_note: Eight rappels down Mile High Club's line on a SINGLE 60 m rope. That configuration is newer than the route: a dedicated rappel line was added alongside Mile High Club in August 2019 specifically so the descent could be done on a single 60, and the eight-station description dates from then. Accounts written before that assume a single 70 m or two 60 m ropes, and counts from that era differ honestly - eight single-rope rappels on a 70, or seven - so an older report disagreeing with this table is describing the pre-2019 descent, not an error. The line stays about 10-15 ft skier's LEFT of the bolt line throughout, and you should prefer the skier's-left anchor wherever two exist, because most stations are doubled so that rappelling and climbing parties are not on the same anchor. Beyond Redlining is equipped for rappelling but its own line is explicitly not recommended: the first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it requires angling rappels off single bolts where many rappels only reach the next anchor on rope stretch. Beyond Redlining's own hardware - a mid-pitch-1 bail station, a missing maillon on pitch 3 - belongs to that line and not to this one. No per-station rappel distances are published for the Mile High Club descent, and the rappel line does not follow the climbing line, so the pitch lengths are not a substitute; the figures given are nominal rather than measured.

set.approach: From the Ohanapecosh Campground day-use area (1,914 ft), follow the Silver Falls Loop Trail clockwise for about 1 mile; the boulder sits right off the trail and is hard to miss. The Silver Falls Trailhead inside Ohanapecosh Campground is closed in 2026 for the Ohanapecosh reconstruction project, so this loop can't currently be started from the campground side — instead, approach via the Eastside Trail from the Grove of the Patriarchs parking lot, picking up the Silver Falls Loop from that end. This is an easy, well-maintained trail with essentially no gain or route-finding difficulty; Ohanapecosh/Silver Falls has running water nearby but none is needed for the short approach itself.

This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent trip reports note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Trail tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft, but the bushwhacking through here is described as minimal. From there, stay on the west side of Freezeout Creek, hiking roughly 50-100 ft above the waterline, which gives the most open going through 5,000 ft. At 5,000 ft, cross to the south/east side of the drainage, where the terrain opens into meadow and talus. Above this, climb steep red heather, talus, and scree to a notch on the peak's southwest ridge at about 7,600 ft. From the notch, the final roughly 700-750 vertical feet to the 8,300+ ft summit is class 2 with short class 3 sections. Total one-way distance from the lakeshore to the summit is on the order of 16-17 miles with close to 7,000 ft of gain from the boat landing alone (the 8,500 ft gain figure reflects the day's cumulative up-and-down, not just net elevation). Freezeout Creek is the reliable water source for essentially the entire approach up to about 5,000-5,500 ft; carry water above that, since there is no dependable source on the upper heather/talus/scree slopes or the summit ridge. Because of the remoteness and boat-access logistics, this is realistically a long single push (18+ hours car-to-car including the taxi) or a one-night backpack, not a casual day hike.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the southwest scree/gully slopes to the 6,300 ft bench, staying off the looser climber's-left skyline gully in favor of the main descent gullies/vegetated slopes used on the way up. Continue down into Chiwawa Basin, re-ford the creek, and retrace the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 and Buck Creek Trail #1513 back to the Trinity Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling anywhere on it — none is typically required. Watch for loose rock and scree underfoot on the upper southwest slopes (a common complaint on nearby Fortress Mountain's gullies applies here too), and in early season the same gullies used for the ascent can be glissaded or skied for a much faster descent when snow-covered.

set.approach: The standard approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft), at the end of Forest Road 6211 off the Chiwawa River Road (FR 62) north of Leavenworth. From the trailhead, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the valley along Phelps Creek, gaining about 1,900 ft over 6.5 miles to Spider Meadows; you enter the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary around the 2.5-mile mark, and Phelps Creek itself is the reliable water source the whole way up (a couple of minor tributary crossings, easy on foot/log in normal summer flow). Beyond the meadows the trail climbs into upper Phelps Basin toward the base of Spider Glacier at roughly 5,300 ft, then ascends the glacier/snowfield about 0.5 mile to Spider Gap (7,100 ft) — this is the crux of the approach: it's a permanent snow/glacier slope that is generally a straightforward boot-pack or plunge-step in summer but can have open crevasses and firm, icy conditions early season, so carry (and know how to use) an ice axe, and microspikes are a common recommendation; whiteout or early-morning refreeze can make an axe/crampons more than optional. From Spider Gap descend the north side — about 100 vertical feet of the steepest snow (softer, less sun-affected snow tends to be climber's-left/north), then scree, then an easing snowfield — down roughly 3.5 miles past the Lyman Glacier and Upper Lyman Lakes to Lower Lyman Lake (~5,587 ft). From Lower Lyman Lake, climb back up through open meadows for about 1.8 miles to Cloudy Pass (~6,438 ft), the normal camp/staging point for the peak. From Cloudy Pass, Cloudy Peak's summit is well under a mile away and about 1,500 ft higher: an obvious boot path leads up through wildflower meadows onto rocky talus, gaining the peak's southwest ridge. Follow the ridge crest itself — straying off it onto the flanking slopes drops you into seriously unstable scree/talus — picking a careful line through loose talus blocks to avoid kicking rock onto anyone below; the ridge has real exposure with a precipitous drop on its far (north) side. At the base of the final summit block, traverse around to its east side and then work around toward the north (back) side to find a walkable weakness through the Class 4+ short scramble to the true summit; this last bit is narrow with real exposure and is the route's technical crux. Three approaches reach Cloudy Pass: besides the line described here, Cloudy Pass/Cloudy Peak can also be reached via the Buck Creek Trail #1513 from the Trinity Trailhead over Buck Creek Pass, or via the Railroad Creek Trail from Holden Village (reached by Lake Chelan boat/vehicle shuttle) past Lower Lyman Lake — both longer, multi-day alternatives to the Phelps Creek/Spider Gap line described above, which is the one matching the round-trip distance (~39.6 km) and the Leavenworth/US-2 road drive.

From the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead (elev. ~3,960 ft, at the end of FR-4300-500 off East Buttermilk Creek Road/FR-43, reached via Twisp River Road west of Twisp), follow the West Fork Buttermilk Trail #411 into the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The trail climbs steadily up the West Fork of Buttermilk Creek through ponderosa pine and larch forest. Expect several unbridged crossings of the creek and its side drainages that can run high and fast with snowmelt through June — plan on wet feet or careful boulder-hopping in early season. Maintenance is light and blowdowns are common in the lower miles in recent years; a GPS track is worth carrying since flagging/tread can thin out where deadfall forces detours around downed timber. At roughly 7–7.5 miles and about 3,500 ft of cumulative gain, the trail tops out at Fish Creek Pass (~7,480 ft), a major junction where it meets the Fish Creek Trail #1248; Star Lake sits just below/north of the pass and is the last reliable water source before the summit push, and a common camp for parties splitting the trip over two days. From the pass, leave the maintained trail and pick up the obvious boot path/climbers' trail that switchbacks northwest up the open ridge toward Courtney Peak. This use trail gains roughly 900–1,000 ft on easy class 2 tundra and talus with a good game/climbers' path most of the way; a few hundred feet below the summit it steepens into larger class 2+ boulders that require careful hopping and some route-finding to the summit block. Snow can linger in the gullies near the pass and on the upper ridge into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early-season (June) attempts. Round trip from trailhead to summit and back runs about 17 miles with roughly 4,700 ft of total gain — this matches a long car-to-car day or an overnight with camp at Star Lake, not the longer Star/Oval combined traverse some parties do as a multi-summit epic.

From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' track from its east end down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak. Then traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin EAST of Cutthroat Peak, where the East Face routes begin.

Avoid the steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall on the way in.

set.descent_text: Descend the same southwest ridge/south buttress line back to the 5,700-5,800 ft saddle, then drop the forested southwest flank back toward Gorge Creek. This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route - most parties, including at least one documented winter ascent, downclimb the entire way with careful footing rather than pulling out a rope; ropework is not standard on the summer scramble. That said, the upper south buttress has a short band of slime-coated, mossy slabs just below the summit ridge, plus a lower cliff band further down the buttress, that some parties choose to rappel instead of downclimb, especially when wet: expect at most one or two short, single-strand rappels (a 30-60 m rope is more than enough for either) off whatever natural anchor is available - a tree, horn, or sling around a block, as there are no bolted or fixed anchors reported anywhere on this route. Below the buttress, glissade or plunge-step the snow gully/talus draw back through about 4,500 ft, then descend the same brushy, deadfall-choked forest line (partly in the 2015 burn) through the cliff-band bypass around 2,400-2,800 ft and back down to the Gorge Creek footbridge and Highway 20. Watch footing on the steep forest sections (parties report significant knee strain) and stay off snow above Point 5,872 or the peak's steep east-facing terrain, which can carry cornices and avalanche hazard well into the season.

set.approach: No route-specific trailhead or approach beta for this boulder problem turned up anywhere online, and the name itself reads like a locally-known or in-joke label rather than a catalogued, widely-documented line — it isn't cross-referenced anywhere against a named boulder or trailhead in the Glacier Peak area. With 0 pitches, no elevation gain listed, and a roughly 1 km/0.6-mile approach distance, this is a short, low-commitment boulder problem reached by a brief, mostly flat walk from a pullout or trailhead rather than a sustained mountain approach. Expect an informal boot-path or use-trail through forest/talus for under a mile with negligible elevation change; watch for the usual approach hazards of the Glacier Peak Wilderness at low elevation — wet roots and mossy rock in the trail tread, and blowdown after storms — but nothing resembling glacier travel, creek fording, or avalanche terrain given the minimal distance and zero gain.
set.descent_text: This is a boulder problem (0 pitches, no rope-length or anchor data of any kind), so there is no rappelling involved — descent is a walk-off / down-climb back to the base along the same short use-trail used on the approach, then out the way you came to the trailhead. Land on pads, spot as usual for the topout, and watch footing on any wet rock or duff on the way down given the low-elevation, forested character of the ground here.

Most parties reverse the route: downclimb the south-facing gullies back to the Eye Col and continue down into Crescent Creek Basin, a mix of class 4 downclimbing and short rappels off natural anchors (rock horns and slings - no bolted stations reported) on loose rock; expect 1-3 short single-rope rappels depending on snow coverage and the exact gully taken. East Twin Needle is frequently climbed in combination with West Twin Needle as part of a Southern Pickets enchainment; in that case parties continue the ridge west and exit via the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch rather than re-descending the Eye Col gullies. That exit is better documented: two rappels using double 60m ropes are needed below the notch to get past vertical slabs, landing on grass and sloping rock around 6,800'; from there the route continues down a south gully with additional short rappels over vertical rock above a lingering snowfield before regaining Crescent Creek Basin. All anchors encountered on this descent are natural (horns, chockstones, slings) - carry cord/webbing for anchor building and expect to leave gear. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: back up and over the Chopping Block ridge, down The Barrier (roughly 3,200' of descent to Terror Creek - loose and brushy, arguably harder in descent than ascent), across Terror Creek, and out the Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.

set.approach: From Barlow Pass Trailhead (end of pavement on the Mountain Loop Highway, elev. ~2,361 ft, 30.5 mi east of Granite Falls), the approach starts on the gated Monte Cristo Road/Old Monte Cristo Townsite Trail — a flat, easy old railroad grade that parallels the South Fork Sauk River for about 4.1 miles to the Monte Cristo ghost town (elev. ~2,750–2,800 ft). This stretch is closed to public vehicles (maintained by volunteers) and has been damaged by past flood events: the original bridge over the South Fork Sauk near the townsite was destroyed, so expect to either ford a side channel (safe in low water, hazardous during rain/snowmelt) or cross on a fallen log — check current conditions before relying on either. From the townsite, pick up the Glacier Basin Trail, climbing steadily alongside Glacier Creek through forest; roughly the last half-mile below Glacier Basin becomes rough, rocky scrambling near a series of waterfalls (Glacier Falls). Leave the maintained trail around 4,200–4,500 ft, just above the falls, where Glacier Creek is easily and safely accessible — this is the last reliable water before the climb. From there it's cross-country travel: traverse talus and heather benches, then steep, brushy timber, toward Foggy Peak's south face/west ridge. Snowline commonly sits near 5,000 ft into early summer, so an ice axe (and possibly light crampons) is worth carrying for the upper approach in June/early July. The final few hundred feet to the summit is a steep class 3 gully with abundant loose, downsloping rock and some route-finding needed to stay at class 3 rather than straying into class 4 terrain; a helmet is strongly recommended for anyone climbing behind another party member. One-way distance from Barlow Pass to the summit is roughly 8 miles with about 4,000-4,400 ft of cumulative elevation gain, consistent with the ~25.75 km (16 mi) round-trip distance.

set.descent_text: There is no walk-off — descend the same West Ridge/couloir line. From the true summit, downclimb back to the notch, then work down the ridge crest with a mix of exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and short rappels off slung horns and blocks (natural anchors, with tat left by parties and a couple of bolted stations reported low in the system, in the gully section climbers nickname the 'Cat Scratch Gullies'). A commonly reported sequence is on the order of 3 rappels — one off the top of the crux tower, a second dropping onto north-side snow, and a 30m rappel (60m rope doubled) through the steepest snow to the top of the upper moat. In late-season, dry conditions, however, multiple trip reports describe needing as many as 6–7 sequential single-rope rappels with a 60m rope to descend the full length of the couloir/gully system to the glacier below, so don't skip any anchor (a couple of the stations are intentionally short) and be prepared to build extra stations if you can't find the next one. In good, consolidated early/mid-season snow, much of the couloir can instead be down-climbed facing in or plunge-stepped, cutting the rappel count to as few as 1–2. Watch for the bergschrund/moat again near the base of the couloir. From the base, reverse the glacier-remnant/talus traverse back to Boston Basin camp and out the climbers' trail to the trailhead; total descent is commonly slower than the climb (reports of ~1.5 hrs downclimbing vs ~1 hr to the summit from the notch).

The documented lower pitches (P1 to a fixed 2-bolt anchor, P2 to ledges) suggest Free Mojo can be descended with rappels using a 60m rope from the fixed anchors if not continuing to the top — a party retreating after pitch 2 would rappel P2 then P1 back to the ground. For the full route to the summit (6 pitches), finish via the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base.

set.approach: Start at the Goodell Creek trailhead (~600 ft, off Hwy 20 near Newhalem, North Cascades NP/Ross Lake NRA). Follow the old roadbed/climbers' path paralleling Goodell Creek for about 4 miles, gaining only ~1,000 ft, to a junction around 1,700 ft marked by a stone/rock arrow, post, and large cairn — this is the standard jump-off for every Southern Pickets objective and the last easy, reliable water before the climb steepens. Here the unmaintained Terror Creek climbers' trail cuts uphill to the right and turns relentlessly steep: a boot-beaten but often faint path gains roughly 4,000-4,700 ft in well under 3 horizontal miles through old-growth forest and brush (expect head-high slide alder/devil's club depending on season and snow year) before breaking out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft onto heather benches, slabs, and snowfields. From treeline, rather than stopping at Terror Basin (the camp used for McMillan/Inspiration/Terror objectives), continue a rising traverse west/northwest staying near the 5,800-6,400 ft band into Crescent Creek Basin — the standard high camp for Frenzel Spitz, Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and the Chopping Block, reached via a steep initial drop into the basin on mixed snow/talus followed by a roughly one-hour traverse. From camp, climb east/northeast onto the ridge to gain the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col; the south (Crescent Creek) side of this col is the comparatively friendlier side — loose but moderate 3rd/4th class scrambling — in contrast to the sustained loose 5th-class terrain that guards it from the north. From the col, downclimb/scramble roughly 500 ft down broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered terrain on the Frenzel Spitz side to reach the base of the South Route proper. There is no dependable water above the Terror Creek junction until snowmelt or tarns near camp, so carry enough for the ~4,500+ ft, multi-hour climb in between; the ~18-mile round-trip distance reflects that this is realistically a long day-and-a-half approach with a basin camp, not a single push.

set.descent_text: Frostbite Ridge is essentially a one-way, committing line — 'no turning back once you hit the ridge' — and virtually all parties descend a different, easier route rather than reversing the ridge. The standard descent is down the Sitkum Glacier: from the summit, descend the gully east of the summit into the upper Sitkum Glacier, traverse and descend to a saddle at roughly 8,000 ft, then continue down the lower Sitkum Glacier to Boulder Basin, picking up the climbers' path back to the PCT/White Chuck Trail and out to the White Chuck River Trailhead (some parties instead reverse to the Cool Glacier/Gerdine Ridge side if that's where their car is staged). The single rappel belongs to the ridge itself rather than to this walk-off descent: guidebook-style route notes describe a natural belay-horn anchor (a rock horn, typically backed by old slings — inspect before trusting) just above the steep ice north of the Rabbit Ears, used to lower one pitch of steep ice into a notch referred to as the 'doorway gap' in the summit rib. This is a single-pitch rappel — a 30m single-strand rope is sufficient for the drop described — encountered while working through the crux ice/rock step near the Rabbit Ears (i.e., on the way up for most parties, since the standard descent avoids the ridge entirely); some parties simul-climb this step with screw/picket protection instead of rappelling, depending on ice conditions. Carry 3–4 ice screws and/or pickets for this section and for the steep snow/ice above the Rabbit Ears regardless of whether you end up rappelling it.

set.rappel_count_note: A four-station sequence of 50/50/50/20 m is sometimes attached to this route. It matches, figure for figure, a published trip report for NORTH Gunsight Peak's West Face — a 5.11+, 6-pitch, 600 ft rock route on a different summit — and does not belong to this Class 5.6 glacier route on the main spire. Nothing about those figures was measured here, so they are not carried. What is documented for this route is two double-rope rappels: "We belayed each other back down the exposed summit ridge, then made a double-rope rappel down the west face", and then "a diagonal double-rope rappel, putting in directional protection along the way, which allowed us to reach the snow finger in one shot." That party carried two 60 m ropes. No single-rope descent of this route is documented.

set.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of the Cascade River Road — gravel/washboard, high-clearance/AWD recommended), climb the well-graded Cascade Pass Trail switchbacks 3.7 mi and about 1,800 ft to the broad 5,400-ft saddle at Cascade Pass. Two standard lines converge on Horseshoe Peak from here, both eventually crossing loose, unmaintained terrain above the pass. Sahale Arm option: continue past the Cascade Pass junction onto the Sahale Arm Trail, climbing the open heather ridge past the Doubtful Lake overlook to Sahale Glacier Camp (about 5.9 mi and 3,940 ft of gain from the trailhead, ~7,600 ft). From camp, traverse east across the boulder/heather plateau below Sahale Glacier (passing roughly a dozen established camp pads), downclimb a steep snowfield (whippet or axe useful, can be firm/icy into midsummer), then traverse east to gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge. Follow a cairned climber's trail down the ridge, negotiating one short 4th-class step, into a scree/talus gully that drops to a snowfield around 6,600 ft. Cross this snowfield into Horseshoe Basin, traverse a wide ledge at ~6,600 ft rising gradually to ~6,800 ft at the ruins of the old Black Warrior mine, then continue on loose scree/talus contouring to a stance south/southeast of Horseshoe Peak below the crest of Ripsaw Ridge. Lower Horseshoe Basin option (more direct, more elevation loss/regain): from Cascade Pass, drop east into Pelton Basin (established camp; reliable water at Doubtful Creek/Pelton Basin — fill up here, since Horseshoe Basin's own water is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk) and work cross-country toward the Black Warrior mine gully, a narrow (~8-ft-wide) rock dike dropping about 100 ft to the Horseshoe Basin side: Class 3 at the top, a short Class 4 downward step to an alcove with old mining equipment stashed in it, then continuing Class 3 but loose and exposed. From the basin floor (~6,600 ft) contour northeast then east on slabs below the Davenport Glacier to reach the base of Ripsaw Ridge below the summit notch. Camping is prohibited in Horseshoe Basin itself, so most parties base at Sahale Glacier Camp or Pelton Basin and day-trip the peak from there — consistent with the ~16.8-mile (27 km) round-trip distance. Either way, expect extended travel on loose talus/scree and slabs with real fall exposure, a snow crossing that wants an axe (crampons in early season), and route-finding by cairn/climber's trail rather than maintained tread once past Sahale Arm or Pelton Basin.

set.descent_text: The Southwest Face (East Peak's low-fifth-class line) is short — 2 pitches — and the standard descent is to rappel the route itself: three rappel stations are encountered descending the line, using natural anchors (slings around the chockstone/horns typical of this rock, not bolts) rather than fixed hardware. Because each pitch is short, a single 60m rope is sufficient for all three raps, though some parties carry a 70m for extra margin/rope-stretch buffer at the lower stations — bring an extra sling or two since anchor material on featureless granite here tends to be climber-placed webbing that may need refreshing. The final rappel lands back past the chockstone into the North-East Peak notch/gully, from which you downclimb and scramble the loose gully back down to the basin above Lake Ingalls, retracing the approach. Watch for loose rock in this gully on the way down, especially if other parties are above. As an alternative some climbers skip rappelling the direct line and instead do a short 4th-class downclimb from the East Peak summit block to link into the main peak's South Ridge descent/rappel line (shared with the standard Ingalls Peak South Ridge route), then talus back to Lake Ingalls — but the three rap stations and short rappel off the summit block point to the direct-line rappel descent as the route's normal descent, which this text follows.

set.approach: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (roughly 1 mile in from the old trailhead gate, elev. ~600 ft), the road has been closed to motor vehicles since a 2002 flood took out a ~300-ft section, but it remains open to foot and bicycle travel — most parties bike the flat, mostly-shaded roadbed to save time, working around the washout on a riverside bypass/use trail. Continue roughly 5.5 more miles of road-walking/biking to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end (about 6.5 mi and ~1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate). From there, pick up the Constance Pass Trail, which climbs steadily south/southwest through forest into subalpine parkland — sources differ on exact trail mileage (roughly 5–8 additional miles depending on where the count starts), gaining to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft; the upper stretch is steep, open meadow and scree with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline and none above. From Constance Pass, leave the maintained trail and travel cross-country west, dropping into the head of Crystal Basin and climbing to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance–Warrior massif dividing the Dosewallips (Crystal Basin) side from Avalanche Canyon. This stretch is talus, scree, and (early/mid-season) lingering snow and ice — the informal climbers' track fades near the pass, so careful route-finding is needed, and a rope/axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass in early season. From Crystal Pass, descend into upper Avalanche Canyon — a barren, glacially carved basin between Mount Constance and Inner Constance — following an intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, staying toward the right (north) side of the canyon past the distinctive 'Cat Ears' rock formation, then contour/climb toward the base of Inner Constance's northeast side. From there, a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the right side of the north ridge/crest on broken, blocky class 2–3 terrain with occasional class 4 (and low 5th class) moves where the crest steepens, working up to the summit. This Dosewallips/Crystal Pass approach (about 16 mi one-way, ~25.75 km) is considerably longer than the more commonly used Lake Constance approach into Avalanche Canyon (roughly 8 mi one-way) but avoids that trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section; expect a 2–3 day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon, and carry all the water you'll need above Constance Pass since only transient snowmelt is available higher up.

Start at the Denny Creek Trailhead (~2,280 ft), reached via Forest Road 58 (Denny Creek Road) off I-90 Exit 47. From the trailhead, follow Denny Creek Trail #1014 north/east up the valley. At roughly 1.2-1.3 miles the trail crosses Denny Creek at the 'Slippery Slab' — smooth cascading bedrock and pools that are the last easy, reliable water source before the climb steepens. Beyond the slab the trail climbs through forest, crosses talus/boulder slopes, and switchbacks up to Hemlock Pass (~3.8 miles, ~4,600 ft), where it meets the Melakwa Lake Trail #1011 junction (the right/east fork continues toward Lower Tuscohatchie Lake). Bear toward Melakwa Lake and descend gently about half a mile to the lake basin (~4.3-4.5 miles, ~4,550 ft) below Chair and Kaleetan Peaks — good campsites and the last dependable water before the summit push. From the lake outlet, leave the maintained trail and follow a well-defined but unmaintained climbers' path that heads steeply northwest, gaining Kaleetan Knoll (Peak 5,700) through subalpine trees, heather, and talus. From the knoll the boot path drops several hundred feet down its west side into a rocky, west-facing talus bowl below the saddle that separates Peak 5,700 from Kaleetan's south ridge; cairns mark the crossing but route-finding can be tricky in cloud or early-season snow. Regain the ridge at the saddle and follow the boot path north, just below/along the crest, for a few hundred yards to the base of an obvious gully/ledge system splitting Kaleetan's south face — this is the standard finish, roughly 400-600 vertical feet of Class 2-3 scrambling on loose, exfoliating rock, exiting onto a short summit ridge with one more brief scramble to the true summit (6,259-6,260 ft). One-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is about 9-10 km (matching the 19.3 km round trip) with about 4,500 ft of total gain. Key hazards: the summit gully and upper shoulder hold snow well into early summer — multiple recent trip reports describe needing an ice axe and light crampons on the northwest-facing finish into June/July; the rock on the upper peak is loose throughout, and exposure increases near the top; and the talus traverse below the Kaleetan Knoll saddle has no continuous trail, so cairn-following and route-finding judgment (especially in poor visibility) are required.

Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20 (milepost ~151, roughly 30 miles east of Newhalem / ~37 miles from Marblemount). Follow Easy Pass Trail (Green Trails Mt. Logan No. 49) 3.5-3.6 miles and about 2,700-3,000 ft of gain to Easy Pass at 6,550 ft — figure 2-3 hours. The trail crosses Granite Creek on a footlog near the start, climbs through about 2 miles of hemlock/silver-fir forest, then breaks into open avalanche meadows and crosses Easy Pass Creek three times before the final push to the pass; steep snow can linger on this upper section well into July and an ice axe is recommended into early summer. From the pass, drop down the North Cascades National Park side to the end of the first switchback, where a faint, easy-to-miss climbers' path breaks off onto Ragged Ridge — this junction is unmarked and is the most commonly botched route-finding point on the whole approach; if you don't spot the boot path, head off-trail toward the ridge anyway. From there, sidehill northwest across scree, talus, grass and blocky terrain at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft along the south side of the ridge (about an hour), crossing one notable waterfall/stream beneath Mesahchie Peak around 6,500 ft on an easy bench — this is the one water crossing of consequence on the traverse and also a reliable water source. Continue to the basin/shoulder at roughly 6,600-6,870 ft just south of the Katsuk-Mesahchie col, known as Ragged Ridge Camp (only two workable flat tent sites; good water draining the basin). A free NPS backcountry permit is required to camp here. From camp, gain a further 200-600 ft to a saddle/bench on the ridge descending from Katsuk's west summit — tedious scree with a short stretch of 4th-class scrambling near the top — then locate the leftward-trending Southwest Gully high on the peak, which runs up toward a mushroom-shaped summit block. Low in the gully, bypass a waterfall by staying on its left (west) side on loose, 'kitty-litter' scree (Class 3). In early season (before roughly July) the entire gully holds steep snow to 45 degrees and demands an ice axe, crampons, and solid snow-climbing technique. Given the ~19.3 km round-trip distance, this is realistically an overnight approach (roughly 7-8 miles and 4,500-5,000+ ft to camp) rather than a single-push dayhike for most parties.

The standard approach follows the North Fork Sauk River Trail (USFS Trail #649) from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (~2,050 ft), reached via Forest Road 49 off the Mountain Loop Highway south of Darrington. The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the river valley for about 5.5 miles to Mackinaw Shelter — a possible camp, though tight for a larger party — crossing several tributaries en route, including Red Creek, which trip reports describe as 'interesting but not difficult' to ford in normal flow (a trekking pole/sturdy stick helps with balance); it can run considerably higher during spring snowmelt or after rain. Past the shelter the trail turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail in a meadow (~6,000 ft) with the first real views of Glacier Peak and the White Chuck/Kololo massif. Turn right (north) on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to White Pass (5,900 ft) — roughly 9 miles and 4,800+ ft of gain from the trailhead, and the last reliable, easy water source before the high traverse. From White Pass the maintained trail ends and the route becomes a boot path: traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin / White River Meadows (~6,300-6,500 ft), the common base camp, either via Red Pass (1.2 miles from the PCT junction) or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck River basin (the 'Foam Pass' variant). From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier — this is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges. From the glacier, gain the flat shoulder at ~6,000 ft, then climb the connecting ridge NNW to a bulge at 7,200 ft, cross a small basin below Kololo's east summit, and continue west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft, from which the ridge forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque leads to the final glacier/talus/ledge scramble to the summit (Class 2+). This is a long approach in its own right — the 46.99 km distance reflects a round trip in the 28-29 mile range — so almost all parties camp at White River Meadows or Foam Basin rather than attempting the trailhead-to-summit push in a single push. There are two long approaches: this North Fork Sauk line, and the alternate White River Trail approach from the east, which reaches a similar high basin by a comparably long trail-plus-cross-country line.
set.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line rather than following a separate down-route: downclimb the summit talus/ledges and upper glacier back to the 7,400 ft saddle, follow the connecting ridge back down to the ~6,000 ft shoulder, and re-cross the White River Glacier, Glacier Gap, and White Chuck Glacier back to Foam Basin/White River Meadows camp, then retrace the boot path over White Pass to the PCT/North Fork Sauk Trail junction and down the switchbacks and river-valley trail miles to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rappel stations are documented on this route, and trip reports describe reversing the glacier-and-ridge line rather than any rope-lowering. The real descent hazards are glacier hazards, not rock hazards: one detailed trip report documents 'fully open' crevasses low on the White Chuck Glacier requiring careful route-finding/crampon work, and a roughly 200-yard section of exposed blue ice ('a shallow icefall') on the White River Glacier that demands careful crampon travel; stay roped for glacier travel on the way down as well as up, and expect snow bridges to be less trustworthy and crevasses less obvious in early season than by late summer. Budget real time for the descent — the same trip report logged about 5.3 hours from summit back to camp alone, before the multi-hour trail hike-out. Glissading may be feasible on snow-filled sections below the shoulder for parties comfortable self-arresting, especially early season, but it is an optional shortcut, not a required part of the route.

set.rappel_count_note: These five stations are the ORIGINAL chockstone/notch descent down the south side, and the count assumes a SINGLE rope for the three upper rappels plus TWO ropes for the chockstone rappel - sources describe it as up to five rappels depending on conditions and the number of ropes carried, and parties with two ropes throughout combine some of the upper ones. The second gully rappel comes up about 5 ft short on a 60 m. IMPORTANT: this is probably not the descent a Labor Pains party will use. A separate BOLTED rappel line was established down the West Face, running between the West Face route and Labor Pains itself, and Labor Pains' own published gear note calls for a 70 m rope specifically to take advantage of those West Face rappels. That line shares only the FIRST anchor with the chockstone descent - from it you head down the West Face instead of into the gully - and has nothing else in common with the stations listed here. It is currently six stations on bolts and chains ending a minute from the base of the routes, with one rappel that a 60 m does not make (parties report needing to block and extend a strand, or carry a 70), and a last anchor that is genuinely hard to find, on a rib below some shrubs and skier's left as you walk down loose dirt from the fifth station. Some parties still rappel from a nearby dead tree carrying no slings, which is not the anchor. Do not blend the two lines: the station list shown is the chockstone line.

set.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — forest along Mountaineer Creek, a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, right at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet (about 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain). Fill water here — it's the last source. Cross the outlet and continue toward the lake's south/east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake, then cut left through dense brush to the obvious base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. From the gully, scramble up a 3rd-class ramp to the actual base of the technical climbing. A documented approach for this route took about 3 hours 47 minutes trailhead-to-base, matching the 3.5-4 hour estimate.

set.descent_text: Because this is a shorter (4-pitch) line on the East Face rather than a full summit route like Liberty Crack or Thin Red Line, the standard descent is the same notch-based line used across Liberty Bell: downclimb east ~100 ft through trees/loose rock to the 2-bolt station, then one rappel to an intermediate stance followed by a double-rope rappel (or two single-rope raps) into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch — 2 rappels on bolted anchors — then downclimb the scree gully to the climbers' path. Note that because this route (like Liberty Crack) is approached from the East Face pullout rather than Blue Lake Trailhead, returning via the west-side notch means either a car shuttle or a roughly 1-mile roadside walk back to your vehicle; parties who top out near Liberty Crack's finish sometimes instead use that route's dedicated 6-bolt rap line or the 4-double-rope-rap line off M&M Ledge to return directly to the East Face base.

set.rappel_count_note: Four rappels off bolts, reached by working climber's LEFT from M&M Ledge, and the description that gives that sequence assumes TWO ropes - four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground. Parties who first rappel from M&M Ledge's own fixed pin-and-wire anchor, which also trends climber's left, count five. No single-rope option is described for this line. The alternative descent, for parties who continue to the true summit rather than rappelling from the ledge, is the standard Liberty Bell notch route - a downclimb east to a two-bolt station and two rappels of about 25 m into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch - which is fewer rappels but lands on the opposite side of the mountain from the East Face approach and from your pack. Per-station distances are not published; the figures given assume near-full-length double-rope rappels.

set.approach: From the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trailhead (~3,500 ft, end of Eightmile Road/FR-7601), follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.5 miles to the signed fork where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) splits left/south. Continue roughly 1.8 more miles — crossing Mountaineer Creek and a boulder-hop stretch near the outlet — to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3 mi in), the last easy, reliable water before the pass. Skirt the lake's south/east shoreline on a braided, cairned climbers' path over talus and slab to the base of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep gully/headwall at the lake's south end. Aasgard Pass is the crux of the approach: it gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on a mix of dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping, cairns are frequently knocked down and the path braids into several use-trails, and well into summer it can still hold firm snow/ice that makes an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) worthwhile even though the route is otherwise a scramble. Top out at Aasgard Pass (~7,800-7,841 ft, ~5.3 mi from the trailhead). Beyond the pass, cross the grey talus/glacial-till 'moonscape' of the upper Core Zone past Tranquil Lake (Lake Freya) and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex some guides call the Brisingamen Lakelets. Near the far end of these meadows watch for an unsigned climbers' path forking right (west) toward Little Annapurna — crossing a stream and passing a toilet sign means you've overshot the junction. From there the route is more a scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths than a trail; pick the path of least resistance up the broad north-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling (low 3rd class at most) to the 8,485-ft summit. Trailhead-to-summit totals run about 15-16 miles and 5,000-5,800 ft. Hazards: no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet, so fill up there; loose rock and rockfall potential on Aasgard Pass and the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun/thunderstorm exposure on the open talus above the pass; and early/mid-season snow on the pass creating slip-and-slide fall hazard.

set.overview: Despite its name and grade label, Live Free or Die! is NOT a boulder problem — it is a full 11-pitch, roughly 1,200-foot free route up Liberty Bell's East Face (grade 5.12- yds; crux may feel 5.12b for shorter climbers), sharing a few meters and belay stances with the Independence Route. Established in summer 2017 by Seth Keena-Levin, Nathan Hadley, and Blake Herrington. Mostly 5.10-5.11 thin face climbing leads to a reachy, bouldery crux sequence ending in a downclimb past two bolts.

set.approach: Lizard Mountain has no dedicated trailhead — the accepted approach follows the southern leg of the Ptarmigan Traverse corridor out of the Downey Creek Trailhead (~1,600 ft) on the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) east of Darrington. Take Downey Creek Trail #768, which enters Glacier Peak Wilderness within the first half-mile and climbs gently through old-growth forest, crossing several tributary creeks (can run high in early season) for about 6.6 miles to the Bachelor Creek Trail junction near 2,400 ft. Turn onto the Bachelor Creek climbers' path — unmaintained, steadily steeper, and notorious for blowdown (expect to step over or crawl under numerous downed trees) plus a brushy alder/slide-alder band around 3,800–4,400 ft that becomes a real bushwhack when snow hasn't flattened it. The trail fords Bachelor Creek itself, which flows fast and cold with snowmelt in early-mid summer — scout for a log crossing or plan on wet feet. Above treeline the trail breaks into meadows near Bachelor Meadows and reaches Cub Lake (~5,340 ft), a reliable water source and common first camp. From Cub Lake, climb a steep, often snow-covered pitch onto Itswoot Ridge (~6,350 ft), another established camp with tarn water. Beyond Itswoot Ridge the route goes cross-country (boot path in season) toward and across South Cascade Glacier — a real glacier with crevasse hazard, especially late-season when snow bridges have opened up; rope travel is prudent unless the glacier is fully consolidated. This crossing tops out at Lizard Col (~6,798 ft), the broad notch on Lizard Mountain's south ridge overlooking White Rock Lakes to the southwest. Trailhead to Lizard Col is roughly 14–15 miles one-way with on the order of 5,000+ ft of net gain (more once the undulating up-and-over-Itswoot-Ridge terrain is counted), so almost everyone treats this as a 2–3 day round trip rather than a day climb — matching the ~29-mile (46.67 km) round-trip distance. From the col, the South Route gains Lizard Mountain's south ridge directly to the summit, a straightforward but loose Class 2 scramble of roughly 600 vertical feet, staying near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the uppermost section is a downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, parties generally find 2-3 more rappel stations working down toward the notch system: a single 60 m rappel to a belay/anchor stance, followed by an overhanging section that's typically rappelled on doubled rope (i.e., a full 60 m rope folded, giving ~28-30 m of rappel) down to just below (north side of) Gunsight Notch/the V-notch. Accounts are not fully consistent on the exact count — some describe essentially 3 key rappels down this line, others log 4, and one description notes '5 rappels will get you down... a 60 m rope is long enough' — the variance reflects rope length used and which anchors parties link together. Plan on 4-5 rappels with a single 60 m rope (or 2x 30 m/60 m doubled) to be safe, and treat 3 as an optimistic minimum if you're able to link stations with a full 60 m strand. Anchors are natural/fixed, not bolted: expect slung trees, horns, and boulders with aging webbing/cord — inspect every anchor before weighting it, back it up if it looks tired, and carry a knife and spare cord/webbing since parties have had to replace or rebuild anchors mid-descent. The first station below the staircase is reportedly in a tree at the top of the drop overlooking the V-notch. Once down to the notch, reverse the snow/scree gully and the traverse back across Mixup's east flank to Cascade Pass and out the trail to the trailhead; if you camped at Cache Col/Kool-Aid Lake, break camp there instead of continuing all the way to the car. Watch for rockfall from parties above throughout the descent, and be alert for a moated-out Cache Col in late season if that's part of your exit.

set.overview: A direct-start variation to the Northwest Face on SEWS, first climbed III 5.11 A1 (with a short section of aid) by Mark Allen, Joel Kauffman, and Tom Smith, October 13-14, 2006; the 5.11b grade reflects later free ascents of the aid section.

set.approach: The Wilson Glacier sits on the east side of Mount Adams, descending from around 10,600 ft to a terminus near 7,400 ft — a less-visited, less-documented flank than the standard south or north-side routes. Parties reach it via the Cold Springs/South Climb trailhead (5,600 ft, FS Rd 8040 off FS Rd 80): follow the South Climb Trail #183 about 1 mile up an old road bed to the junction with the Round the Mountain Trail, then instead of continuing north toward Lunch Counter, follow Round the Mountain Trail east and then north, contouring below Crescent Glacier and around the mountain's eastern flank toward the Wilson/Klickitat glacier basins — a long, mostly-off-trail traverse with route-finding, creek crossings, and exposure to rockfall directly below the headwall's cliff bands. Given the route's distance (~27 km) and gain (6,700 ft) roughly match the other long approach routes on this mountain, expect a full day just to reach a camp near the toe of the Wilson Glacier before a summit attempt.
set.descent_text: The descent reverses back down the South Climb to Cold Springs: after topping out via the headwall, parties traverse over toward the summit plateau and descend the standard South Climb route (non-technical snow/scree walk-off, good glissading in early season) back to Lunch Counter and out to the Cold Springs trailhead — a different, easier line than the ascent. This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent. Because the Wilson Glacier Headwall itself is steep snow/ice below cliff bands, a party that needs to bail mid-face rather than finish over the top could reasonably rope down using pickets or V-threads in snow/ice, but this would be an improvised retreat, not a documented standard rappel.

Descent is a reversal of the ascent line, not a walk-off in a different direction: downclimb the same diagonal west-face ramp back down to roughly 4,000-4,300 ft, re-enter the gully/cliff-band system, and pick back down through the brush and slide-alder benches to regain Illabot Creek, re-crossing to the south bank near the same spot used on the way up before following the fisherman's path back to the Arrow Creek trailhead. There is no cairned or maintained route for most of this, so route-finding is the primary descent hazard — it's easy to drop into the wrong gully in the cliff band, and carrying a GPS breadcrumb of your ascent (or flagging key turns) is standard practice. The heather- and moss-covered rock on the ramp is more hazardous descending than climbing since holds face the wrong way and the exposure reads more obviously on the way down; a short, steep, exposed Class 3 section near the top of the ramp is where a party might reasonably choose to place a hand line, though this is discretionary, not standard practice. This is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed anchors, no bolted rappel stations, and no established rappels — crampons are occasionally useful on lingering snow patches, but a rope is not standard.

set.approach: Getting to the trailhead is currently part of the approach: a 2023-24 washout closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at the Madison Falls parking area, and as of the NPS's 2024-2025 advisories that closure adds roughly 7 miles each way of road walking or biking just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road remains open to foot/bike traffic beyond Madison Falls). From Whiskey Bend, the actual hike-in follows the Elwha River Trail, a well-graded historic path along the river's east bank that passes the old Geyser Valley homestead sites (Michael's Cabin, Humes Ranch) in the first mile or two. The trail is mellow by Olympic standards, staying under roughly 2,000 ft of gain through its first 15+ miles, and passes Lillian River junction (~4 mi), Mary's Falls Camp (8.8 mi), Canyon Camp, Elkhorn Guard Station, and Stony Point as it winds upstream through old-growth forest with the Elwha River itself as a constant, reliable water source. Camp Wilder and Hayes River Guard Station mark roughly the trail's halfway point. Continue south to Elwha Basin and Chicago Camp (roughly 24-26 trail miles from Whiskey Bend), where the Elwha River must be forded — NPS explicitly flags this crossing as one to check conditions on beforehand, since it can be genuinely hazardous in early-season high water or after rain. At and beyond Chicago Camp the maintained trail effectively dissolves into the Elwha Basin, and travel becomes cross-country: a boot-beaten climbers' path continues up the valley headwaters toward the obvious white tongue of the Elwha Snow Finger, a permanent, avalanche-fed snowfield filling the bedrock gully that leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,763'). The Snow Finger is the standard way through this section — carry an ice axe and know self-arrest. Recent trip reports note the snowpack has been thinning in late summer, exposing an opening moat, running water under the snow, and rockfall funneling off the surrounding walls, so climb it early in the day and reassess if it looks broken up; NPS notes snow can linger above Chicago Camp into July. From the top of the Snow Finger at Dodwell-Rixon Pass, Mount Dana sits several miles east-northeast (its coordinates place it roughly 5 miles from the pass, closer to the Mount Norton/Elwha-headwaters side of the range than to the main Carrie-Ferry-Pulitzer crest). There is no path here; parties pick a line across talus, heather benches, and lingering snow patches toward Dana's western slopes for the final class 2 scramble to the 6,214' summit. Water becomes scarce above the pass, so carry enough for a high camp. Given the roughly 70-mile round-trip distance, this is realistically a multi-day trip (3+ days) with a high camp near Dodwell-Rixon Pass or in the upper Elwha basin, not a car-to-car push, and solid off-trail navigation skill is essential once you're past Chicago Camp.

There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then climbing/sidehilling toward Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face known as "the Catwalk"; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and sets up a cleaner entry onto the Fairchild Glacier. Access the upper Fairchild Glacier around 6,700 ft; rope up and put on crampons here (ice axe mandatory most of the season), then follow a wind-formed snow ridge running down the glacier — similar to the Hogsback on Mt. Hood — to stay clear of crevasses, with a steeper 35–40° exit section near an icy patch before gaining Fairchild's summit ridge and the 6,899 ft summit. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Fairchild Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel.

set.overview: Mount Hardy (8,099 ft, or 8,097 ft depending on the survey, within normal survey variance) sits in the Okanogan Range of the North Cascades above the headwaters of the Methow River, just west of Methow Pass on the Pacific Crest Trail and ~1.75 miles southwest of taller neighbor Golden Horn (8,366 ft). It's composed of rapakivi-textured Golden Horn batholith granite (same body as Golden Horn, Tower Mountain and Azurite Peak) and is a prominent, easily-seen summit from SR 20 between Washington and Rainy Passes. Sidney Schmerling and Hermann Ulrichs made the first recorded ascent in 1933; the name was officially adopted in 1973.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent descent route. Downclimb the short summit east ridge back to the south/southwest ridge, then follow that ridge and its heather-and-scree slopes back down to the low saddle point between Mazama Dome and Mount Herman. Drop off the ridge on the same cross-country line through the scrub-tree band and heather slopes to rejoin the maintained Chain Lakes Trail (682) at the last switchback below Herman Saddle, then follow Chain Lakes Trail and Bagley Lakes Trail (684.1) back past Bagley Lakes to the trailhead. This is a walk-off scramble with no rappelling required under normal summer/dry conditions — 0 rappels. The main descent hazards are loose, down-sloping scree and talus on the ridge and connecting slopes (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below), and lingering snow in the gully/ridge-traverse sections in early season, where an ice axe and/or microspikes are a reasonable precaution; a rope is not standard gear for this route.

Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling. The final summit block (roughly 150-200 ft of terrain) is mostly class 3 but includes one well-documented 15-20 ft class 4 step (a shallow crack, often marked by a cairn) that parties downclimb facing in; no fixed rappel anchor has been reported here in any trip account reviewed, so treat this step as a careful downclimb or build a natural (gear/sling-around-block) rappel only if your party is uncomfortable reversing it. From the summit, retrace the class 2-3 talus/boulder terrain back down through the notch below St. Peter's Gate, drop back down the rock rib (losing the ~800 ft gained above the lake), and return to Lake of the Angels. From the lake, pick the way-trail back down into the basin and rejoin the maintained Putvin Trail, reversing the hand-line/headwall section around 4,200 ft (the single trickiest spot on the descent when wet or in the afternoon sun on lingering snow) and then the long steep 4-mile descent to the trailhead. Parties on this route (rated S5/T5) log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car-to-car with breaks — budget a full day and start early since the lower trail is exposed and hot in the afternoon. One cautionary note from a trip report: at least one party mistakenly took a steep mossy/waterfall gully as a descent shortcut off-route and found it far worse than reversing the ascent line — stick to the known up-track rather than improvising a shortcut.

set.approach: From the Hoh River Trailhead (end of Upper Hoh Road, roughly 18 miles east of US-101 south of Forks), follow the Hoh River Trail upriver — a well-graded, mostly flat rainforest path through old-growth Sitka spruce and big-leaf maple for its first ~12 miles. Checkpoints: Mount Tom Creek camp (~mile 2.5-3, elev ~600-700 ft), the first spot with real views of Mount Tom's icefields across the valley; 5 Mile Island (mile 5); Happy Four shelter camp (mile 5.8); Olympus Guard Station (mile 9, water plus a ranger kiosk, with the High Divide/Bogachiel Peak junction 0.6 mile beyond); Lewis Meadow (mile 10.3); and Elk Lake (mile 14.8, elev ~2,500 ft), the last reliable camp and a common high-camp/turnaround point. Past Elk Lake the trail steepens hard, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in the final 2.3 miles to Glacier Meadows (mile 17.1-17.6, elev ~4,200-4,300 ft), the standard high camp for both Mount Olympus and Mount Tom objectives. Around mile 17.5 a major washout forces a fixed-ladder descent/crossing (roughly 100 ft, rope-assisted, one person on the ladder at a time) — treat this as the approach trail's own crux hazard, not just a nuisance. From Glacier Meadows, take the Lateral Moraine Trail (~0.8 mile, +800 ft) up onto the moraine crest for the first full view of the Blue Glacier and the terrain beyond; a shorter Terminal Moraine Trail (0.4 mile) offers an alternate viewpoint. From the moraine, glacier travel begins: descend onto and cross the (crevassed) Blue Glacier roped as a team, then climb the broad snow dome (Snow Dome) that most Olympus parties also ascend. Rather than continuing toward Olympus's summit, the Mount Tom line splits off Snow Dome and traverses horizontally along the snowy upper massif, staying below the main Olympus peaks, until it connects with Mount Tom's own White Glacier (on its NE slope) or drops via the Hubert Glacier on the south side to reach the Mount Tom-Olympus connecting ridge. Expect open crevasses on both the Blue and White/Hubert Glaciers requiring standard roped glacier travel, and a final class 3-4 scramble over loose rock to the summit block. Water is abundant along the Hoh River Trail itself (river and creek crossings throughout) but is glacier-melt/snowmelt only above Glacier Meadows, so plan treatment accordingly. The round-trip distance (~69 km/43 mi) reflects the long valley approach plus the extended high-massif traverse to Tom and back — well beyond a standard Olympus summit day. An alternate approach comes from the Bailey Range side: follow the Sol Duc River/High Divide trail system to Cat Basin, then the off-trail Bailey Range crest (over Stephen Peak, Mount Pulitzer, Mount Fitzhenry, and Ferry Basin) to reach the Mount Tom-Olympus col area, rather than via the Hoh River/Blue Glacier.

Park at the Cascade River Road washout roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount, about 100 yards past the Cascade River crossing near the FR 1570 junction (signed for Kindy Ridge/Found Lake). The old FR 1570 spur is now permanently closed to vehicles, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek at roughly 1,150-1,400 ft — trip reports note the washed-out culvert and downed timber (one log up to 4 ft across) blocking the road about 0.8 mile in. Follow the old road/boot path about 1.5-1.75 miles, crossing several windfalls, to an old firepit near a reliable creek (last easy water before the ridge). From the firepit the unmaintained climbers' path turns steep immediately, threading old-growth forest on exposed roots with occasional spur tracks around blowdown; expect the tread to fade into debris in places — this stretch to the Found Peak area (roughly 2.5 miles, gaining ~2,500-3,000 ft) is the main route-finding crux of the approach. The path dips to a broad saddle near 4,800 ft where the boot path is easy to lose; parties often end up scrambling 300-400 ft above the pass before relocating the trail, then follow it up through grass and boulders (~600 ft) into a meadow with Found Lake below (pools here are not reliably potable). From there the route climbs over Point 5695 and drops to a second saddle before joining Kindy Ridge proper: a broad, mostly open granite ridge combining faint tread and easy slab-hopping, steep but non-technical, with constant views toward Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and the Cyclone Lake basin. Camps are commonly made near 6,200 ft on the ridge or down at Cyclone Lake (a strikingly turquoise tarn-fed lake); a small stream south of the ridge camp and a tarn just above Cyclone Lake are the best water sources up high. From the ridge/Cyclone Lake basin, Mutchler Peak's summit block is reached by heather and blocky rock slopes rising out of the basin — moderate Class 2-3 scrambling with some loose rock near the top; total car-to-summit distance is on the order of 12-14 km one way given the ~24.8 km round trip, consistent with reports citing full Snowking/Kindy Ridge trips of 15-17 miles round trip and 6,500-7,100+ ft of cumulative gain. Because the approach is entirely unmaintained (no official trail, no numbered Forest Service trail), competent off-trail navigation is required, and this is a long, full-day-plus approach — most parties treat it as an overnight rather than a single push.

Start at the Blue Lake Trailhead, a small pullout on SR-20 just west of Washington Pass. Follow the main, well-graded Blue Lake Trail through forest for about 1.5 miles. Watch for a cairned, well-worn climbers' boot path splitting off uphill to the right toward the Liberty Bell group cirque — this junction is easy to miss if you're not watching for it. From the split, the climbers' path steepens considerably, switchbacking up talus and heather benches beneath Concord and Lexington Towers. Budget roughly 1.5-2 hours and about 1,900-2,000 ft of gain from the trailhead to reach the Concord-Lexington col (the notch between the two towers), which is the start of the North Face route. Snowmelt trickles low in the basin can provide water in early season but are unreliable by mid-to-late summer — carry water from the trailhead. Lingering snow/firm névé in the upper gully approaching the col is common into early summer and may warrant an axe or traction.

set.overview: A committing 1,800 ft, 9-pitch IV 5.9+ line up the lowest/leftmost corner of Sloan's West Face, first climbed by Mike Preiss and Mark Bunker in 2000. After two funky, thinly-protected opening pitches you're essentially committed to finishing the route and descending the far side of the mountain.

set.approach: Hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) from the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road) — 4 miles and 2,280 ft gain, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at 1.5 miles and staying right at the Lake Stuart Trail junction — to reach Colchuck Lake (2.5-3 hours). Unlike the west-side routes, the NW Ridge is approached from the east side of the lake: work around the eastern shoreline/talus to the base of the obvious gully that splits toward the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, the granite spire between the lake and Colchuck Balanced Rock. Ascend this gully (loose in spots, rope-up terrain for the upper section) to the notch, then move onto class-3 ground on the NW Ridge proper before the climbing begins. One documented ascent clocked roughly 4,760 ft of total gain and a 12-hour car-to-car day, consistent with the route's ~18.5 km round-trip distance.

Trailhead: Slate Pass (~6,900 ft), the end of the Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) just below Slate Peak lookout — this is a full backpack approach, not a day hike (~13 miles/1,400+ ft one-way to base camp, within the ~28-mile round trip). From Slate Pass, drop off the pass on the old trail/way-trail toward the Whistler Cutoff Trail; this initial descent can hold snow well into summer (some parties carry an ice axe for it). The Whistler Cutoff Trail is an easy, well-graded downhill cruise to the Middle Fork Pasayten River, which is crossed unbridged — typically only ankle-to-shin deep in normal summer flow, but ford with care during early-season snowmelt or after rain. From the ford, join the Robinson Creek / Eureka Creek Trail system and follow it roughly to the Fred's Lake cutoff around the 9-10 mile mark; trail tread is in generally good, brush-free condition to this point.
