At the Shellrock Trail junction the maintained tread ends — travel beyond here is on a rougher, sometimes brushy path with blowdown. Climb past Fred's Lake to 7,100-ft Rolo (Fred's) Pass, then descend/contour a short, sometimes cliff-banded slope (route-find carefully here) into the Lake Doris basin (6,975 ft), a good camp with reliable water and the standard base camp for Osceola. From camp, leave the trail and go cross-country roughly 0.6 mile northeast through open forest, then talus, gaining about 1,400 ft up Osceola's long southwest-facing scree/talus slope to either the southwest ridge or south face. The south face is a slow, tedious boulder/talus slog; a faint but real climbers' trail on the southwest ridge (roughly 48.828, -120.583) offers noticeably better footing and is preferred by parties who've found it. Final scrambling to the 8,584 ft summit is Class 2-3. Watch for wet, lichen-covered rock on the upper slope, which gets slick fast in any moisture.

set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent for most parties: from the summit, downclimb the Class 3-4 gully/ledge system on the peak's east side back toward the snow finger and glacier. Where the ledges pinch down at a dihedral feature (a damp, water-streaked corner reported by climbers), most parties do NOT free-downclimb the full corner — instead, build two rappels (roughly full 30m/60m-rope-length pitches) down the dihedral to regain the glacier below. Anchors are natural (slung horns, chockstones, or gear placements) rather than fixed bolts/chains — this is an alpine line with no fixed hardware, so carry a small rack and cordage for anchor-building and expect to leave gear (or plan to down-lead/simul on lower-angle sections to save equipment). A single 60m rope handles both rappels; parties without a 60m would need to break it into more, shorter rappels. Some parties instead find they can downclimb the full chimney/ledge system without rappelling if conditions and confidence allow (reversing the ascent by downclimbing is the lower-commitment option), but the two-rappel dihedral descent is the more commonly reported method, especially when the rock is wet or holds are snow-covered. Below the glacier, retrace the approach: descend the Valley of the Chiefs (or, per at least one report, an alternate line down the main Overcoat drainage through open trees to avoid waterfall-forming cliffs lower down), re-ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and rejoin the Dutch Miller Gap Trail back to Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the bike/hike-out to Dingford Creek Trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully/dihedral and for the river ford being higher/colder in the afternoon on hot days from glacier/snowmelt runoff.

set.approach: There are two real approach options for the South (Southwest) Route on Phantom Peak, and both are serious multi-day North Cascades bushwhacks — this is not a trail hike. Option one, the Luna Creek approach: from Ross Lake Resort, take the water taxi across Ross Lake (roughly $35, saves about 6 miles of paddling/road-walking) to the Big Beaver trailhead. From there it's about 14 miles of maintained, mostly flat, forested trail up the Big Beaver Creek drainage (through old-growth cedar groves and past beaver ponds/marshy sections) to Luna Camp, an established backcountry campsite where a NOCA wilderness permit is required. From Luna Camp the trail effectively ends; climbers leave the maintained tread and push cross-country up the Luna Creek drainage toward Phantom Peak's south side, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft over a few miles through some of the worst brush in the Cascades. Fred Beckey, on the first traverse through here in 1940, called it 'the worst imaginable struggle with flies, devil's club, willows, and alder' — modern parties confirm little has changed, reporting huckleberry, devil's club, vine maple and slide alder so dense that 0.5 mph is a good pace, plus heavy mosquito/fly pressure in summer. The creek itself must be forded in places; fords get harder (deeper, faster) the lower/farther downstream you are, so it's best to gain elevation out of the valley bottom as early as possible rather than fighting the brush along the creek itself. Water is abundant throughout (the creek and countless side-seeps), but hazard is really the terrain: no trail, no cairns, high fall-into-a-hole-in-the-brush risk, and real potential to get separated from a partner in the thick stuff (this has happened to real parties here). Above the brush line the drainage opens into subalpine meadow and talus below Phantom's south aspect. Option two, favored by several recent parties, comes from the north via Whatcom Pass: Hannegan Trailhead (3,100 ft) → Ruth Creek Trail → Chilliwack River Trail (includes a cable-car creek crossing) → Brush Creek Trail up to Whatcom Pass, then off-trail via the Whatcom Glacier and Perfect Pass to a base camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From that camp, the route to Phantom itself is a roughly 1,000-ft descending traverse east across snow/talus to the base of Phantom's broad southwest buttress, then up a snowfield to a saddle around 6,100 ft within the buttress — this saddle is effectively the start of the technical climbing. Whichever approach is used, expect 2-3 days of travel each way; the total round-trip distance (51.5 km / ~32 mi) reflects the Big Beaver/Luna Creek option's mileage.

From the Longmire Wilderness Information Center (2,762 ft), pick up the Wonderland Trail heading southwest. About 3 miles in, after climbing out of Longmire, the trail drops steeply (~400+ ft) to a log-bridge crossing of Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically damaged or washed out by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier, so check current status at the Longmire WIC before you leave, since a failed crossing can force a long reroute. Beyond the creek the trail climbs by switchbacks through old-growth forest, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek, and traverses a ridge past Devil's Dream backcountry camp (~5 mi, reliable water) before breaking out of the trees into the subalpine meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 mi and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin and open views of the Tahoma/South Tahoma icefall. From Indian Henry's, leave the maintained Wonderland Trail and follow the Mirror Lakes spur/climbers' path west (several plank crossings over marshy meadow, then end of maintained tread), continuing cross-country onto the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak between about 6,000 and 6,300 ft to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. Running water is often available here from snowmelt puddles into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at ~6,300 ft (with running water nearby) is another common first-night camp for a 2-day ascent. From Point 6631, drop briefly NNE to a saddle at about 6,400 ft — the start of Success Cleaver proper. The lower cleaver is a loose, choss-and-scree slog with short bursts of class 3 scrambling and real rockfall exposure from parties above; there's no single obvious line, so expect route-finding. Travel improves noticeably higher up onto firmer rock and (early season) continuous snow, following goat tracks. Many parties place a second high camp on the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft (snow platforms can be dug in), from which the route continues up the crest — including a knife-edge section that requires real scrambling once snow melts off it — before angling climber's-right up snow gullies that merge onto the Kautz Cleaver around 12,200–12,600 ft, then up steepening snow/ice (to roughly 45°, with an isolated ~15 ft step near 55° used to bypass a cliff band in some seasons) to Point Success at 14,158 ft. All-in this is roughly 12–13 miles and 8,000+ ft of gain from Longmire to Point Success, so most parties split it over 2 days with an intermediate camp rather than going car-to-car in a single push.
set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than continuing on to Columbia Crest and taking the more heavily-trafficked Disappointment Cleaver off the mountain (a carry-over option some parties choose, but it requires crossing the summit crater and arranging a shuttle back to Longmire from Paradise). Down-climb the snow/ice below Point Success back onto the Kautz Cleaver chutes near 12,200–12,600 ft, then drop onto the Success Cleaver crest and retrace the loose, scree-and-choss cleaver back down to the 6,400 ft saddle by Point 6631. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no fixed rappel anchors or established rappel stations documented for this line: Success Cleaver is one of only two Rainier routes with no significant glacier travel, and it's descended on foot (ice axe, and crampons in icy years for the upper snow/ice step) rather than by rope, so the rappel count is 0. Main descent hazards are rockfall and underfoot looseness on the cleaver (worse below other parties, and worse late-season as snow recedes and exposes choss), plus sun-softened snow in the gullies by mid-morning — parties who carry over report the Disappointment Cleaver snowfield turning 'amazingly sloppy' by 10 a.m., and the same afternoon softening affects the Success/Kautz Cleaver snow, so plan an early start and be off the steep snow before it goes punchy. From Point 6631/the Pyramid Peak saddle, retrace the cross-country line to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, then follow the Wonderland Trail back through Devil's Dream, back across the Kautz Creek log bridge (check crossing status again), and down to Longmire.

set.overview: Ruth Peak (~6,850 ft; 6,841 ft by some accounts) is the third-highest summit in the Bailey Range, a remote sub-range of the northern Olympic Mountains, between higher neighbors Mount Carrie (6,995 ft, 0.9 mi NW) and Mount Fairchild (6,900 ft, 0.9 mi N). The Fairchild Glacier drapes its northeast slope. There is no trail to the summit — Ruth Peak sits deep in cross-country terrain south of the Sol Duc/High Divide country and is almost always climbed as a waypoint along the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone objective. First ascent 1961 by Bert Brown, Roy Etten, and Victor Nelson.

set.approach: From the White Chuck River Trailhead (end of FR 23, ~2,300 ft, reached from Darrington), follow White Chuck River Trail #643 up-valley through old-growth and second-growth forest along the White Chuck River. There are several tributary creek crossings (some bridged, some not) in the first few miles — treat them with caution in early season or after rain. At roughly 5.5-6 miles you reach the site of the old Kennedy Hot Springs / Kennedy Guard Station (~3,300 ft); the springs themselves were largely buried by debris in the 2003 flood and there are no facilities, but it remains a natural rest/camp point. Continue about 1.5 miles farther, fording Sitkum Creek, to the junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (~3,850 ft) — this crossing can run high with snowmelt in June/July. At the PCT junction, look for a cairn marking the start of the unmaintained but well-trodden 'Sitkum Trail' climbers' path, which switchbacks steeply east up a forested-to-heather ridge, gaining roughly 1,800 ft in a little over a mile, to the campsites of Boulder Basin (~5,700 ft) — the standard base camp, with reliable water from snowmelt tarns and streams through midsummer. Total distance to Boulder Basin is roughly 9-11 miles with 4,000-4,500 ft of gain. From Boulder Basin the route goes cross-country and onto glacier: head southeast onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier, staying in the corridor left (north) of the rock rib/icefall that splits the lower glacier, then trend northeast up-glacier to a broad saddle at approximately 9,500 ft immediately east of Sitkum Spire. The upper Sitkum Glacier carries real crevasse hazard in both its lower and upper sections — rope up for glacier travel, carry standard crevasse-rescue gear, and expect more open crevasses by late summer. From the saddle, a short, loose pumice-and-rock ridge scramble (class 2-3 with a class 3-4 step near the top) leads to the summit block of Sitkum Spire itself. Route-finding on the broad, featureless summit plateau and glacier can be tricky in flat light or whiteout — a GPS track or careful compass bearing is worthwhile. Note separately that FR 23 access to the White Chuck River Trailhead has a history of washouts/closures (2003 flood, and more recent 2025 flood damage) and should be checked for current status before relying on this approach.

From the South Arete base (reached via the Blue Lake Trailhead climber's trail, about an hour in), head down and right along the base of the wall, eventually dropping away to skirt steeper terrain, to reach the start at double cracks beside a fir tree — about 10 minutes of scrambling/traversing from the South Arete. The Hitchhiker begins roughly 100 ft further along the same traverse.

set.overview: Begins near the low-center of the south face at an obvious layback hand-crack (5.10, can be wet). Climb up and left to gain a rising ramp, then exit rightward in the upper section on fun 5.7-5.8 rock, topping out on the west ridge near the summit. Also cataloged as 'South Face Left', the FA is Mike Preiss & Don Preiss in 2004.

set.approach:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), about 30 miles west of Winthrop and a quarter mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass is required and the small lot fills early. Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left, marked by a large cairn.

The South Face routes are reached from the CONCORD-LEXINGTON notch, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord col that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. Rather than trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers; higher up, a reasonable climbers' path appears along its left side and is better than fighting up the gully bed. It sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.

You are at the right saddle when Concord is on one side of you and Lexington on the other, and the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges rather than a steep crack system. If you are facing a crack system, you are at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and looking at the North Face.

There is no approach detail specific to South Face Center beyond this shared approach.

Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (elev. ~3,120 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FS-32), reached via the currentRoadDriveNote's drive. From the trailhead, follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 gently up the Ruth Creek valley (views of Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge) for about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to 5,050 ft Hannegan Pass — this stretch is straightforward, well-graded, and has reliable water at Ruth Creek crossings for the first couple of miles. At the pass, leave the maintained trail: a boot path/climbers' route (watch for a cut-log marker at the unsigned junction — parties have noted the turnoff is easy to miss) breaks off toward Easy Ridge rather than continuing down to Boundary Camp/Chilliwack River. From here it is sustained cross-country travel: climb onto and follow Easy Ridge itself, a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge crest with limited shade — flowing water is available relatively early on the ridge but the FA party warned this stretch 'would be brutal later in the season and in dry years.' Continue along/over Easy Peak (a common first bivy, roughly a full day, ~10 hours, from the trailhead) and then descend/traverse past the notch known as Imperfect Impasse, before regaining elevation to Challenger Col on the flank of Mt. Challenger. From Challenger Col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque (glacial terrain — rope/crevasse-awareness recommended near the pocket glacier) toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, a typical second bivy site, avoiding lingering snow at Pickle Pass. From this high camp it is a further, mostly straightforward cross-country traverse across the western slopes to the base of Spectre Peak's south ridge, reached around sunrise on what is effectively day three. In total this is roughly a 46-mile, ~17,500 ft round-trip approach-and-climb outing (74 km), typically broken into 2 or more travel days each way with route-finding, glacier travel, and off-trail ridge scrambling throughout — this is genuinely one of the longest, most remote approaches in the North Cascades, not a simple hike-in.
set.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb roughly 600 ft of 3rd-class terrain with a couple of low-5th-class moves (the FA party called the upper section 'glory 5.0 terrain') back down through the ridge's hoodoo/tower section. Within that section is the route's key rappel: a single ~30-meter rappel from the final hoodoo tower down to a grassy ledge system. A second, lower rappel of about 25 meters has also been reported past an exposed gendarme roughly at the Pitch 7 band on the west side of the ridge — parties should carry a single 60m rope (or two ropes) and be ready for up to two short technical rappels, though in some conditions the lower one can reportedly be avoided/downclimbed. No fixed anchors are documented on this obscure, first-ascent-era route; expect natural gear anchors (horns, cracks, slung blocks) rather than bolts, and back them up — this is remote, low-traffic terrain with essentially no fixed hardware. Below the rappels/downclimbing, the descent drops onto Spectre's east-facing slopes back toward the Challenger Col/Easy Ridge approach line; in the FA party's heavy-snow-year, early-season conditions this was continuous, 'super chill' steep snow (glissade-friendly with an ice axe and the usual steep-snow/glacier caution), letting them avoid the 'typical endless scree and loose talus' that this face otherwise holds in leaner, later-season conditions — parties visiting in a low-snow year or later in the season should expect a much looser, scree/talus descent instead of snow travel. From the base, retrace the approach line back over Challenger Col, past Imperfect Impasse, along Easy Ridge, over Hannegan Pass, and out the maintained trail to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead — effectively a full reversal of the multi-day approach, not a same-day walk-off.

set.approach: Start at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead (~4,875 ft) on SR-20, 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass (~6,600 ft, ~4.9 mi) — this stretch has only intermittent small streams, so top off water here, since little reliable water exists again until Snowy Lakes. From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass (~6,600 ft, roughly 6.5-7 mi from the trailhead); this pass holds snow into July/August, and when snow-covered it's steep and exposed enough that an ice axe (and comfort self-arresting) is warranted. Beyond Granite Pass the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut, blasted-out section, loses a bit of elevation, and climbs again to Methow Pass (~9 mi). Roughly 10 miles in, just past Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers'/use path branches right (east) off the PCT and climbs ~0.5 mi and ~400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin — Lower Snowy Lake (~6,600 ft) or Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700 ft) — the standard base camp, with reliable water and good tent sites; most parties backpack in and climb from camp rather than going car-to-car. From camp near Lower Snowy Lake, head cross-country south toward Tower Mountain on a climbers' path, then make a short but strenuous traverse across a talus field, aiming for a distinctive large reddish boulder partway across. Beyond the boulder, a ramp on the left side of a large cave (which cuts about 25 yards into the mountainside and makes a good wind-sheltered rest stop) leads up to the base of the main summit gully — from here the route follows ledges on the gully's right side, zigzagging back toward the gully-notch in the ridge and up broken rock to the summit. Total distance to the base of the gully runs roughly 10-11 miles one-way with about 2,800-3,000 ft of net elevation gain from the trailhead to camp (cumulative gain over the Cutthroat/Granite/Methow pass rollercoaster is closer to 4,200 ft). The gully itself is the route's main hazard: the rock is notoriously loose and rockfall-prone, so helmets are strongly recommended and parties should climb one at a time, staying right and moving efficiently through the narrowest sections.

Park at the large paved turnout at the first hairpin turn on SR-20 (North Cascades Highway), about 1 mile east of the Washington Pass summit (roughly 5,160 ft elevation). There's no formal trailhead sign or numbered trail here — the route to Kangaroo Pass is an unmaintained but well-cairned climbers' path on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land along the edge of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. From the pullout, head south/southeast toward the base of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch (below the north side of Kangaroo Temple). Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus field and follow cairns carefully — this lower boulder/talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the approach, especially if snow-covered early in the season. The tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail once you're in the upper basin. Continue up mixed talus, boulders, and open slope to Kangaroo Pass (6,671 ft), gaining about 1,500 ft over roughly 1.5 miles — typically 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only reliable water source on the approach; there is none higher, so top off here. Expect lingering snow from about 5,800 ft up to the pass into early-mid summer, depending on the year — an ice axe and/or microspikes are worth carrying into July. At Kangaroo Pass, leave the boot path and turn northeast onto Wallaby Peak's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail continues briefly then disappears on rock; stay on or near the ridge crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree, and grassy benches. At about 7,400 ft, swing around onto the south flank into the south-facing summit gully. This gully is moderately steep with notable loose rock and scree — wear a helmet, especially with more than one person in the party, since climbers above can kick debris down onto those below; some parties pick a short Class 3 line on the gully's margins to avoid the worst of the scree. Near the top of the gully, exit left (northeast) for the short final scramble to the true summit. Total distance is about 3.0 miles one-way (6.0 mi / ~2,900 ft round trip, or 9.7 km); budget roughly 2 hours car-to-pass and another hour pass-to-summit.

Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone trailhead off SR-20 just west of Newhalem (this is the drive-in endpoint — see road note separately). From the trailhead, follow the climbers' path up the old, overgrown Goodell Creek logging-road corridor through open forest for roughly 3.5 miles; beyond the fork where the maintained tread ends, the route becomes a boot path through talus with only sparse flagging, so follow cairns rather than a continuous trail. This talus/boulder-hopping stretch leads to a crossing of Terror Creek — look for a cairn marking the ford; water levels are seasonal and the crossing can go from a rock-hop in late season to a genuinely wet, current-fed ford in early summer or after rain. Beyond the creek, the route climbs a steep, brushy rib known informally as 'the Barrier': tree debris, slide alder, and a faded, easy-to-lose boot path make this the route-finding crux of the approach. Water becomes scarce above about 5400 ft — expect only dry streambeds and the occasional small puddle, so treat any water below the Barrier as your last reliable fill-up. The path tops out and drops about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin, then traverses roughly a mile north across scree to the common Southern Pickets camp below Mount Terror at about 6050 ft, fed by two streams coming off the slabs above (reliable water and the standard base camp for this side of the range). From camp, West Twin Needle's south side presents two gullies right of a dividing buttress; the true line follows a minor rib on climber's left of the rightmost gully (which cliffs out in a closed chimney) up to the Himmelhorn–West Twin Needle notch at about 7400 ft. The technical crux of the approach is pitching through this 'Eye Col' gully past large chockstones on low 5th-class rock, including one narrow-crack pitch typically taken on a belay. From the notch, easy slabs and scrambling (roughly 5.7) lead to the summit. Total round trip from the trailhead runs about 19.5 miles (~31 km) with well over 7000 ft of gain. Expect loose rock throughout the gullies, sustained route-finding through brush and scree, exposed scrambling on the connecting ribs, and unreliable water above the Barrier.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the south face scramble back to the notch/col below the true summit — Class 3 terrain with one short Class 4 section near the top. Multiple parties report finding rappel slings wrapped around a horn/block just below the summit, used to bypass the single 5.5 step-up/short face move that guards the final scramble to the top (the route also involves jumping a 4-ft summit slot). That is 1 rappel: parties not comfortable downclimbing the 5.5 move typically rig one short rappel (roughly 40-60 ft — easily covered on a single strand or on half of a doubled 60m rope) from a natural sling anchor on the summit block down onto the upper south face, then downclimb/scramble the remaining Class 2-3 ground to the col. There are no bolts reported on this route; anchors are natural (slung horn/block) and should be inspected or backed up, as sling material left by previous parties can be sun-weathered. Note also a short but airy step across a gap on an exposed ledge encountered by at least one party partway down the face — straightforward when dry but worth caution if wet or icy. From the col, reverse the approach line: descend the scree/goat-trail gully roughly 2,200 ft back to Aasgard Pass (plunge-stepping or glissading any snow with an ice axe in hand), then continue down through Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake and out via the Colchuck Lake Trail/Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the trailhead. No additional rappels are needed below the col — the rest of the descent is a hike/scramble walk-off.

set.approach: Park at the Thirtymile Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of West Chewuch Road, about 29 miles north of Winthrop. From there follow the Chewuch River Trail #510 north, staying close to the Chewuch River; Chewuch Falls is a good landmark around 2.5 miles in. Around mile 8 to 8.8 the trail crosses a 2001 burn area — standing dead snags are common here and more prone to falling in wind, so be alert in storms. At roughly 8-8.8 miles (~4,700 ft) reach the signed junction with Tungsten Creek Trail #534 and turn right (northeast). Follow Tungsten Creek Trail #534 for 6.2 miles, gaining about 2,100 ft, passing within earshot of Big Horn and Horseshoe Creeks and crossing Cinch Creek; Tungsten Creek itself, which the trail follows for its final stretch, is the last dependable water before the high country (in dry years, e.g. a September 2017 trip, sources beyond here were reported as dry streambeds and stagnant pools, so tank up). This trail ends at its junction with the Boundary Trail #533 at the historic Tungsten Mine Camp (~6,750 ft) — old mine structures, iron pipe, and building ruins from the 1908-1920s tungsten operation are visible on the south side of Wolframite Mountain. This point is roughly 14-15 miles in, effectively a full day's hike, and most parties camp near here rather than pushing to the summit and back in one day. From the mine camp junction, follow the Boundary Trail #533 west/south for about 1 mile to the point where the trail bends south toward Apex Pass. Leave the trail here and ascend off-trail, heading northeast up Wolframite's broad, gentle west slopes to the 8,136-8,137 ft summit; done on this line the terrain is a straightforward Class 2 talus/heather slope, though other lines or variations can involve short sections of low Class 3. This is the safest and most recommended line up the peak. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is roughly 16-17 miles with about 4,700 ft of cumulative gain, consistent with the ~34-mile (54.72 km) round trip — treat this as a backpack with a high camp near Tungsten Mine or the Boundary Trail, not a single-day car-to-car scramble.
